definition: In computational linguistics, word-sense induction (WSI) or discrimination is an open problem of natural language processing, which concerns the automatic identification of the senses of a word (i.e.
details: meanings). Given that the output of word-sense induction is a set of senses for the target word (sense inventory), this task is strictly related to that of word-sense disambiguation (WSD), which relies on a predefined sense inventory and aims to solve the ambiguity of words in context.

explainer.lead: Word-sense induction automatically identifies the senses of a word, producing a sense inventory rather than consuming one. It matters because it is an open problem distinct from disambiguation, which relies on predefined senses.

tiers.eli5: Instead of being told the meanings of a word, the computer groups the different ways it's used and names the clusters itself.
tiers.practitioner: Researchers induce senses by clustering occurrences of a word rather than classifying into existing labels; a pitfall is that induced senses must be reconciled with the predefined inventories disambiguation relies on.
tiers.paperLevel: An open problem of computational linguistics whose output is a set of senses for the target word; it is strictly related to word-sense disambiguation, which depends on a predefined sense inventory to resolve ambiguity in context.

explainer.example: Collecting many uses of the word 'bank' and clustering them yields separate financial and river-edge senses without any prior dictionary.
